common_name: Green Tower Boxwood (Narrow Columnar Formal Accent Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Tower's naturally narrow, upright form holds its column shape with minimal shearing, useful for flanking an entry or doorway without the width of a rounder boxwood.

directions: Green Tower is a narrow, strongly columnar boxwood selected to grow tall and slender rather than wide, holding a tight, formal vertical shape with only light shearing rather than the heavy pruning needed to force a rounder boxwood into a similar form. Its fine-textured, deep green foliage provides year-round structure for flanking an entry, punctuating a formal border, or standing as a pair of vertical accents where a wide shrub would crowd the space. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; occasional light shearing in late winter or after the spring flush keeps its narrow profile crisp.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Boxwood Selection for the South

common_name: Graham Blandy Boxwood (Extremely Narrow Columnar Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Graham Blandy's extremely narrow form makes it useful in tight spaces where even standard columnar boxwood cultivars would be too wide.

directions: Graham Blandy is one of the narrowest columnar boxwood cultivars available, growing tall and slender in a tight, almost exclamation-point form that fits spaces too narrow for other upright boxwood selections, such as flanking a narrow gate or walkway. Its fine, deep green foliage provides the same year-round formal structure as other boxwood but in a distinctly vertical, space-saving silhouette that needs little pruning to maintain. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; because its narrow form relies on strong vertical growth, avoid heavy shearing that would disrupt its naturally columnar habit.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Boxwood Selection for the South

common_name: Dee Runk Boxwood (Narrow Upright Columnar Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Dee Runk holds a narrow, upright form with less shearing than most boxwood cultivars need to maintain a vertical shape.

directions: Dee Runk is a narrow, upright boxwood cultivar valued for holding a clean columnar to slightly conical shape with less regular shearing than most boxwood needs to stay vertical, making it a practical choice for a formal hedge, allee, or paired accent planting where a consistent narrow profile is wanted over many years. Its dense, deep green, fine-textured foliage gives year-round structure, and its somewhat broader base than the very narrowest columnar cultivars gives it a bit more visual heft as a specimen. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; light shearing in late winter or after the spring flush keeps the form crisp if a more formal look is wanted.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Boxwood Selection for the South

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fastigiata is one of the older, classic narrow upright boxwood selections, used for generations in formal European-style gardens.

directions: Fastigiata is a long-established, classic narrow upright boxwood cultivar, its name referring to the fastigiate, columnar branching habit that has made it a staple of formal European-style garden design for generations, typically used in matched pairs or rows to frame an entry, path, or formal parterre. Its dense, deep green, small-leaved foliage gives the same year-round structure as other boxwood cultivars while holding a taller, narrower profile than rounded forms. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; light shearing in late winter or after the spring flush maintains a crisp, formal outline.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars

common_name: Vanilla Spice Summersweet (Large-Flowered Fragrant White Clethra)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Vanilla Spice tolerates wet, periodically flooded soils and works well in a rain garden or pond-edge planting in dappled shade, the same conditions as other Clethra alnifolia selections.

directions: Vanilla Spice was bred for unusually large flower spikes, nearly twice the size of the species, packed with small white, intensely sweet-scented flowers that open in mid-to-late summer and draw heavy pollinator traffic from bumblebees, honeybees, and butterflies during a period when many other shrubs have finished blooming. Like other summersweet selections it forms a dense, suckering, upright shrub with glossy dark-green foliage that turns clear yellow in fall, and its fragrance carries well through a partly shaded garden on a warm evening. Keep soil consistently moist in partial to full shade, since summersweet does not tolerate prolonged drought, and expect the shrub to slowly spread by suckers to form a colony over time, useful for naturalizing a moist, shaded area.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
